entries.title: The Internet Is in Crisis
entries.summary: For 15 minutes, the celebrity-gossip blogger Perez Hilton livestreamed his violent self-harm without anyone intervening.
entries.content:
For 15 minutes, the celebrity-gossip blogger Perez Hilton livestreamed his violent self-harm without anyone intervening.

Almost 20 years ago, I had tickets to see Amy Winehouse perform in London, at a show that was canceled just an hour before it was scheduled to start. A friend and I went to a nearby hotel bar instead, and not much later, in walked Winehouse herself—tiny, grubby, and completely incoherent. She walked over to us and stared, her eyes both furious and vacant, until someone in her entourage came and dragged her away. I remember the person who flashed to mind in that bizarre moment: the gossip blogger Perez Hilton.

If you weren’t regularly online during the late 2000s, it’s hard to explain how dominant a presence Hilton was—how incessantly he posted about what celebrities might be doing on any given day, how shameless he was about posting upskirt photos, how judgmental his tirades about young women in crisis were. His fiendish MO was lifting pictures from paparazzi agencies and then scribbling penises or obscene epithets on them in order to claim fair use. Hilton—whose real name is Mario Lavandeira Jr.—was particularly cruel about Winehouse, who was being photographed by the celebrity press almost daily in states of disarray. He posted, by turns, about her physical appearance (“super skinny, dirty and wasted”), false rumors of her pregnancy (“We were sure that her ovaries were too gin-soaked to be of any use”), and a performance in which she wasn’t wearing underwear (“Grrrossss!!!!!!!!! Who needs to see cracked out snatch?”).

PerezHilton.com was relentless and brutal, and its readers could not get enough, especially when the blog’s coverage collided with moments of calamitous celebrity breakdown. (When the actor Lindsay Lohan was arrested in 2007, the site reportedly received 8.8 million pageviews that day.) Since then, the internet has metastasized into something officially kinder—we no longer berate famous people in crisis for sport quite as much as we used to—and quietly more appalling, where irony-poisoned young men broadcast their executions and social-media companies seem to basically shrug in response. And so, on Tuesday night, during what seemed to be a mental-health breakdown of his own, Hilton was able to stream himself live on TikTok cutting himself with a knife for about 15 minutes before his broadcast was finally interrupted.

Any number of Hilton’s followers on TikTok could have clicked on the stream thinking they were going to see a standard broadcast about Ariana Grande or Trader Joe’s ready meals (both of which Hilton had posted about on YouTube in recent weeks). Instead, they got a scene of unimaginable violence. “I am fine with horror/gore, have seen a lot real and fake, and this was so deeply disturbing I could not get the image out of my head all night,” one commenter posted on Reddit. Another added, “I watch cartel torture and beheading videos with no issues. I had to turn the perez video off after about 20 seconds, and I felt deeply disturbed for hours.”

TikTok’s failure to interrupt Hilton’s broadcast for such a long time, even as horrified viewers were reporting it, is astonishing. (A spokesperson for the site told Wired that a “moderator error” caused a delay in removal; another told Vanity Fair that Hilton was persistent in his attempts to broadcast what he was doing, using several different streams to do so.)

In the United States, Section 230 of the Communications Act shields technology and communication companies from being held legally responsible for third-party content that appears on their platforms. And since Facebook launched livestreaming in 2015, social-media sites have struggled to establish safeguards for atrocities being broadcast in real time, to the point where the phenomenon of people livestreaming their own attempts to die has become “an emerging public health crisis,” in the words of psychology researchers. After a man livestreamed himself killing 51 people at two mosques in New Zealand in 2019 on Facebook Live, Facebook said it was investing in “technical innovation” to prevent people from abusing its platform. Nevertheless, footage of mass shootings and other atrocities proliferates globally before befuddled tech companies can tie their shoes.

The tone of the contemporary internet is also darker and more nihilist than it has ever been. “Social-media platforms—and especially X—have loosened their grip on moderation at the same time that AI tools have allowed for the easy proliferation of slop,” my colleague Charlie Warzel wrote earlier this year. “Never before has there been so much cynical, cruel content and trolling.”

But the idea that Hilton might end up turning self-harm into content feels particularly fraught. A statement from his family posted online said that the influencer had been “experiencing a severe mental-health crisis,” and that his three children, his niece, and his sister were at home with Hilton when he began hurting himself, although they left immediately “to protect the children from witnessing any further trauma.” Over the past decade and a half, Hilton has tried to pivot away from the bilious celebrity coverage that made him so successful: In a 2010 video, he announced that he would no longer be cruel. But his popularity never quite recovered, and he argued in his 2020 memoir, TMI, that the toxicity of his site was what had appealed to his readers, even if they didn’t want to admit it to themselves: “The more snarky names I gave the celebrities, the more penises or coke or boogers I drew on pictures of them, the more people visited my page.”

It’s also true that PerezHilton.com peaked in its cultural relevance around 2007, the year that celebrity after celebrity seemed to be breaking down in public while pursued by paparazzi on mopeds. That year, Britney Spears shaved her head (when the actor Heath Ledger died in 2008, Hilton sold T-shirts emblazoned with the words Why Couldn’t It Be Britney?), Anna-Nicole Smith overdosed on prescription medication, Lohan was arrested for cocaine possession, Paris Hilton went to jail, and Mischa Barton was arrested for driving under the influence of alcohol. Hilton documented each of these moments in vivid and elaborate detail—my browser finally quit when I got to page 79 of his archives related to Amy Winehouse—because he understood what people wanted from him and his work. “When Britney Spears was at her wildest, people were glued to my website,” he wrote in TMI.

It’s impossible to know whether this awareness informed what he did to himself this week, and how he did it. Hilton’s breakdown is desperately sad; I’m haunted by the idea of what his children might have seen happen in their home, but also by the idea of what all children might see, at any time, in this hopelessly corrupted and seemingly unsalvageable internet.

If you are having thoughts of suicide, please know that you are not alone. If you are in danger of acting on suicidal thoughts, call 911. For support and resources, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or text 741-741 for the Crisis Text Line.

entries.title: The Case for Calling People on the Phone
entries.summary: We’ve never had more ways to keep in touch. So why are we talking to one another less?
entries.content:
We’ve never had more ways to keep in touch. So why are we talking to one another less?

This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning.

Conversation has become optimized—but not always for the better. We send a quick text instead of making a call, react with an emoji instead of a laugh, and turn catching up into a series of efficient updates. Although staying in touch with people is easier than ever, we spend surprisingly little time talking to one another.

“No one picks up the phone anymore,” Alexis C. Madrigal wrote in 2018. That’s in part because too many faceless telemarketers have our number, and in part because more people have come to treat phone calls as something to reserve for emergencies or bad news or major life events. However, in many cases they’re the easiest way to have conversations that texting can’t quite convey—ones that meander, surprise you, and leave you feeling a little more connected than before.

Texting has made communication faster and more efficient, but not necessarily more conversational. Today’s newsletter is a reminder that you don’t need a reason or an agenda to call someone you’ve been thinking about.

On Conversation

Talk to People on the Telephone

By Amanda Mull

It’s time to start calling your friends again. (From 2019)

Why No One Answers Their Phone Anymore

By Alexis C. Madrigal

Telephone culture is disappearing. (From 2018)

Another Symptom of Growing Isolation

By Olga Khazan

A recent study found that people spoke fewer words a day in 2019 than in 2005.

Still Curious?

  • The tension that defines modern life: Most people have a smartphone. But many want to use it less, Julie Beck writes.
  • Maybe don’t send that voice note. The audio messages can encourage selfishness—unless you use them gracefully, Jacob Sweet argued in 2024.

Other Diversions

PS

My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “My sense of awe for this world comes from my backyard, where a family of barred owls nests each year and produces angelic chicks that begin their lives playing among the trees,” Bonnie B. from Cordova, Tennessee, shared. “They make me believe in the magic of life.”

We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks.

— Rafaela

entries.title: Sadism and a Blue Bunny
entries.summary: Not everyone who has a child is fit to love them.
entries.content:
Children are made for love. From the moment they are born, they rely on their caregivers for everything they need, and they need a great deal: warmth, nourishment, grooming, contact. Their lives depend on it. Caring for children often comes at the expense of a caregiver’s personal comfort, which is a trade-off best done out of love.

For a time, newborn children do not realize that they are distinct from their parents, which is reasonable, given that they have not been for very long. But as they grow, they come to recognize that they are individual people, and they begin to consider exploring the world beyond the safety of a caregiver’s arms. Such ventures are exciting, but also somewhat intimidating. Children need a way of transporting their caregivers’ love with them as they move about. For this, they rely on what childhood-development specialists call transitional objects, which allow children to move from oneness with their parents to nascent independence. These objects can include blankets as well as stuffed animals and other toys. In the case of the toddler daughter of Representative Max Miller, this love and comfort took the shape of a blue stuffed bunny.

But only adults call these items transitional objects, and only adults ascribe to them their clinical significance. For children, they are magical talismans cathected with love. They are more than their physical reality—more than cotton or fleece or polyester plush. They are individual and irreplaceable. They have unique powers to soothe. They have meaning. They have names.

When I was a child, I could not sleep unless I had my bunny blanket, a castoff from my older brother’s collection of baby bedding that began life as a yellow quilt with eyelet fringe and became, after hundreds of tumbles in the washer and dryer, a tattered beige slip of a thing. It traveled with me to college and to graduate school, and even now rests folded in my linen closet. For my younger daughter, comfort came in the form of a rainbow scarf that we tucked into her backpack before she set off to her first day of school.

Children are made for love, but not everyone who has a child is fit to love them. Miller, a 37-year-old Republican in Ohio, has been accused of domestic violence by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, according to court filings in their custody battle after a two-year marriage. Moreno, who is the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio, alleges that Miller scalded her with hot water, held a gun to her head, and pushed her into a wall, causing her to hit her skull. She has said that she can’t rule out whether he broke their daughter’s collarbone and bruised her shoulder. Miller denies ever having been violent with his wife and child. At his request, the House of Representatives’ ethics committee has announced an investigation into the allegations against him. Senator Moreno and other congressional Republicans have called on Miller, who is running for reelection, to resign.

Children who grow up in unstable environments tend to rely heavily on the softness and comfort of beloved toys and blankets. According to Miller’s ex-wife, their daughter sought comfort in her blue stuffed bunny. And this bunny, according to court documents, is what Miller took away from her.

In excerpts of emails and texts among Moreno, Miller, their lawyers, a parent-custody coordinator, and Senator Moreno published by Mother Jones, Miller appears to regularly hold his daughter’s bunny hostage, sometimes for days at a time, despite his ex-wife’s pleading and his ex-father-in-law’s diplomatic efforts to retrieve it. In one exchange, Moreno asks if their daughter could “please have her bunny back? She’s had it since birth, sleeps with it every night, carries it with her around the house … Please don’t punish” her, she begged, “if you’re upset with me.” The couple’s custody coordinator wrote to Moreno at one point that because Miller “adamantly” refused to relinquish the bunny, Moreno should plan on keeping it at her house to “avoid these situations because unfortunately in a high conflict divorce these situations blow up often.” (Miller responded on X by asking Moreno to “please stop the lies,” and insisting that their daughter “got her bunny back in 14 hours.”)

In her texts, Moreno appears to allege that Miller’s infliction of suffering upon their daughter is purely instrumental, a way of inflicting pain on his ex-wife by proxy.

When someone else’s pain pleases you, it is called sadism. There is no sound way to manage sadists in society, as normal behavioral incentives do not seem to apply to them. This makes them dangerous. They should probably not spend much time around other people. And they certainly shouldn’t be around children, who can’t defend themselves and can’t understand how someone might thrive on suffering, because children are made for love.

entries.title: How Social Media Makes Our Lives Smaller
entries.summary: In the posting era, there’s room only for redemption and improvement narratives.
entries.content:
In the posting era, there’s room only for redemption and improvement narratives.

Most people spend more time than you think agonizing over their social-media posts. Kathryn Jezer-Morton wanted to understand their thinking—and when she dug deeper, she learned that redemption and optimization narratives are what the algorithm rewards, and therefore what drive the stories we tell. What does that mean for how we all think about ourselves? Charlie Warzel talks to Jezer-Morton about how authentic has become something different from true, and how people’s arcs on social media tend to point only upward.

The following is a transcript of the episode:

Kathryn Jezer-Morton: No one’s interested in scientific data as much as they’re interested in a really compelling anecdote. And this is just attention-economy stuff. This is because a really compelling anecdote is going to perform better for a number of reasons, whereas a big, longitudinal study is gonna have some interesting findings but it’s also gonna have some contradictory findings. Science is often much less, kind of, explosive than, like, this one dude who’s like, I took this supplement, and six months later, I am freaking jacked. You know, that’s cool.

Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain, a show where, today, we’re going to answer a seemingly unanswerable question: How is social media changing the way we understand ourselves and even humanity as a whole?

By any account, I’ve been a somewhat prolific poster for at least two decades. Like most Millennials, I was a kid and high schooler in the pre-social-media days and went to college just as Facebook was taking off. This is partially why, as I’ve long argued, Millennials like myself are often uniquely tortured about social media: We’ve experienced it profoundly shaping our social lives, our culture, our politics, and ourselves, but we can also remember just enough of a time before it that we can see this process as something that was emergent. In other words, it’s not a given that our lives had to be mediated this way, by these massive platforms for viral advertising.

And so a few years ago, I was talking to another writer who is roughly around my age about what it’s meant to come of age in the attention economy. We talked about how fun and experimental all of this was at first, how exciting it was to be connected to everyone all at once. It was both intimate and incredibly public. But also about how quickly all the experimentation turned into something different; how we, without really even noticing it, began writing, posting, and performing—all for this imagined audience. And how we started imagining how that imagined audience would respond. How we’d see people get mocked or shamed or lavished with praise and internalize all of that in the back of our minds. How the way we spoke changed on specific platforms as the result of in-jokes, memes, and a shared culture that everyone was building at once.

This wasn’t necessarily a bad thing, though there are countless examples of the way that social media curdles people or pushes us to be the most neurotic, reactive, and uncharitable versions of ourselves. All these versions once felt separate from our actual selves, but over time they’ve become harder to untangle.

This is the subject of a new book by the writer Kathryn Jezer-Morton, titled The Story of Your Life: How Social Media Shapes the Way We Experience Everything. Jezer-Morton, argues that social media’s greatest influence might be how we understand ourselves as humans and not, as many critics have argued, its impact on attention spans or our politics. Humans are storytellers and always have been. And those stories help us understand the world and our place in it. I was drawn to Jezer Morton’s book in part because of her framing of social media: as a place where all of us who post are telling a collective story about what it means to be a person in today’s world.

In some sense, this is all obvious enough. But what’s less clear is what these platforms and stories are doing to all of us, whether you share your life on social media or you just lurk there. Are they making us more unique or more the same? What is highlighted in a culture that is mediated by algorithms, and what lived experiences are excluded? If social media is the lens through which we capture the story of our lives, is the aperture being widened or narrowed? Jezer-Morton brings a nuance to this polarizing topic, and she joins me now to talk about it all.

Warzel: Kathryn, welcome to Galaxy Brain.

Kathryn Jezer-Morton: Thank you, Charlie.

Warzel: So your book is about social media, but it’s really about how we make sense of ourselves and the world through personal stories. And so I wanted to start with you telling me just a bit about your own personal story growing up on a commune in Vermont and specifically how you feel that shaped your understanding of personal and communal narratives and how it’s sort of a foundation for some of your work in this book, but also on social media in general.

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, so I spent a lot of my childhood on a commune that my dad was part of the founding group of in southern Vermont, and I lived there on and off for a number of years. And I think that, for me, I was always really aware that it was a story. The whole place was a story. I knew that people lived together who weren’t family and that the place had this kind of rich history and that also like we were, kind of—we were hippies, and it was messy, and it was very, kind of, it was a bit of a chaotic vibe some of the time. And so I was being told these stories from when I was very young. And I think that it gave me this really rich understanding that a lot of what life is is storytelling. So when I got to college and we started using social media, I was like, This rules. This is so fun. I am like, I’m a natural. This is like, I was born to do this. And I really just took to it like a fish to water. And I think it was because I was like, No, this is what we do. We narrate ourselves. We bring ourselves to life through pictures and stories. And you know, it’s like a fun creative project. We’re basically narrating ourselves into being, and we get to do it however we want. But I think that as soon as I started using it, I was like, What are we all doing, though? Like, what are we actually up to? And from the very beginning—like I think I joined Facebook in 2007—I was like, This feels like there’s something going on here, and I think we’re doing something and we don’t even really know what we’re doing.

Warzel: Let’s go back a little, though, to you loving social media. I mean, one thing that’s very clear from your work is that genuine affection and also that, like, I’m not trying to tell you that posting is bad or that you know your screens are destroying you just because they’re there all the time. But I wanna go back to this. I have a very similar relationship to social media. It’s tortured, but it’s also, especially in the beginning, I was like, Wow, you made this thing for me. This is like—all I want to do is perform for different people and create this persona. What was part of the story you were crafting? What were you trying to do very early on in those, like the halcyon days?

Jezer-Morton: So I was freshly graduated from college. I was living in New Orleans. I was married. I was living this little professional life. And I think it was an opportunity to show the world, like, Check it out, guys. Like this is me and my little life. And it was very Millennial. There’s something very deeply cringe about it, looking back, like, Here’s my house, and Check it out. We made gumbo. It was so fun.

And you know, Here’s Mardi Gras. Here are our costumes. And it was also—I was living very far away from my family, and so there was a practical aspect where I was like, Look at my life in New Orleans, guys. And New Orleans is a cool place, and it photographs well. So it was easy. But I think I was just honestly becoming an adult and becoming independent and telling everyone that I was happy about that. And I think I was doing a little bit of nascent personal branding in that I wanted to seem fun but also like an adult, like I was independent.

Warzel: You devoted your academic career in part to understanding how these feeds shape us, and this led you to do anthropological work of interviewing normal people about their social-media use. And you say that you’ve been fascinated by how little people want to discuss what they do in their feeds. And I found that really, really interesting. Why do you think that is, that people kind of balk at examining what it is they’re doing? ’Cause we’re spending so much time on these platforms.

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, to me that was what got me started writing this book. I was like, No one wants to talk about it. And yet we’re doing it for a public audience. So, right, what’s going on when you choose this picture instead of that picture and post it? I know it’s not just automatic behavior because I’m thinking about it. I mean that’s really where it started. I was like, If I’m thinking about this, if I’m being careful with my messaging, then everyone else is too. And we never talk about that. And it’s also very, I think, in a kind of puritanical sense or something, like it’s embarrassing to admit that we are really kind of working hard to project a certain image.

No one really wants to admit that. And everyone accuses other people of doing that. And no one self-implicates. So that was really the starting point of like, I want to sit with someone and be like, talk to me about your feed. Tell me what you’re doing. It’s okay. It’s just you and me. Just tell me what you have going on. And what I found was a lot of people were like, “No one’s ever asked me this before.” And if I could gain their trust, they were like, Yeah, man, let’s get into it. I actually have a lot—I think about this a lot.

Warzel: So okay, broadly speaking, what is it that you think we’re all doing when we post?

Jezer-Morton: So I just want to begin by saying that, obviously, if this is—it is the world, social media. So it is enormously diverse and there are gonna be exceptions always. So I can’t say everyone’s doing the same thing. I think that what we’re doing is we’re maintaining a brand that we have built over time. Each of us has one.

It’s an identity. There’s a sort of consistency that we’re seeking to maintain. And we’re just working in the service of maintaining it. And I think, for some of us, it might be something that we’re a bit tired of. Maybe we kind of started working with this brand at the beginning of our social-media time and we’re kind of stuck with it. And maybe we’re not posting anymore because we’re like, I just like, I don’t want to keep doing that thing anymore. That shtick is old. Like, I can’t.

Warzel: Mm-hmm.

Jezer-Morton: But a lot of us are just like, Yeah, I’ll just keep doing it, basically. And it’s to do with demonstrating that you have your life under control, that you have a certain degree of fitness in your life, whether that’s economic or physical—just, like, you’re really with it; you understand the world; you can kind of handle the world as it’s coming at you. I think it’s about capacity. You’re basically proving your capacity to survive, day after day or however often you’re posting. And yeah, I think that’s what people are doing. And I don’t think that’s how it started, and I think that’s how it is now.

Warzel: How would you describe that evolution? Because the way that I think about it, from my own perspective, I think from what you were just saying about stumbling onto these platforms and figuring out is: It was so light. It was so experimental, right? It was, Okay, I’m gonna do this. I’m gonna try on this piece of my persona. It all felt like it had no consequences, right? Just like very intimate stuff that’s happening, very public, but also ephemeral and light and like, This is my Facebook persona, right? This is how I am on Twitter at, like, being a young journalist—I’m speaking very personally—like, on the town in New York City doing fun stuff, working for this company, BuzzFeed. It was all very low-stakes, I guess I would say. And then something happened. But how would you describe the evolution of what happened as these platforms became more mature?

Jezer-Morton: I think that the movement away from the chronological newsfeed was really huge. I think that once an algorithm was starting to feed us stuff based on its performance, it changed. I think users clocked to that really quickly. And I think that we just started to learn that some stuff got seen and other stuff didn’t. And we did start, I think—not everybody—but I think a lot of people started to change ever so slightly the way that they posted.

People came to understand that selfies or pictures of themselves performed better. I think that just the idea of being visible in this huge population changed the dynamic. Remember, when we started using these things at the beginning, it was just people that we knew. And I think for most people it still is. Like, you know, you’re a journalist, so you have people who are following you just for your work.

But it’s also like, over years and years, you go through different jobs, you move. So you have these people now who are following you and seeing your stuff who you’ll never see again and who you haven’t seen in years. So they’re effectively strangers. And I think that that changes it too, where you’re like, Okay, so there’s my friends, but then there’s all these random people that are looking at me. And I think even if you’re a person who has no professional business on social media, you’re not selling anything, you’re not maintaining anything, whatever—you’re still talking to strangers. And I think that forces a certain formality, a certain kind of concern for your reputation that was not present at the beginning at all.

Warzel: I wrote this story in 2020 about boomers on Facebook, right? It was all about, like, these boomers are being radicalized on Facebook. And I talked to a lot of them, and one of the things that they described to me that I thought was so fascinating is, especially for boomers—like, for us who are relatively around the age of college while we were on it or whatever, it was like we were meeting people at parties and adding them on Facebook, right? Or something like that. But for the boomers, it was like, Oh my gosh, that was the kid who lived down the street from me 50 years ago, and I can reconnect with them. And there was a magic to that, and it was great.

But once the newsfeed shifted less away from the personal updates into the political updates, you would see stuff like, Oh god, my next-door neighbor from 50 years ago is an incredible bigot, and now I need to argue with them. Right? And so all these people were just exposed to essentially strangers because the relationship was so tenuous to begin with, even though it was so exciting to uncover. And so much of this conflict had happened because, really, you weren’t supposed to be hanging out with that person, right? Or like having that person then comment on a photo of your grandchild. Where you’re like, What gives you the right, man? There’s all this conflict.

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, these are not people that you have any business being in contact with. There’s no utility to these points of contact. They’re unprecedented socially. And so now we’re having to deal with it. And I would say, yeah, younger people have the same thing where it’s like, even really younger people like Gen Z, they’re meeting, churning through tons of new connections. You know, 15-year-olds will have 1,000 people on Snapchat. And it’s like, How do you know that many people at your young age? That’s how it works now. And it just creates this totally nonsensical social environment. Yeah.

Warzel: So you mentioned the phrase personal branding earlier, talking about what people are doing and how social media has pushed people into really thinking like a brand. I think of branding obviously as a way to sell something. What do you think people are selling, and why are they forced into that specific behavior of posting the way that, you know, Wendy’s posts on Facebook, or whatever. Why did people sort of become more like the brands instead of—I mean, I guess the brands have become more like people too—but why do you think that that fusing has happened?

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, it’s true that the brands have become more like people. The people have become more like brands. And now we’re all kind of in this weird middle place.

Warzel: It’s great.

Jezer-Morton: I think that, first of all, it’s just the affordances of the platform. I think the platform, the designs, the interfaces encouraged us to do certain things. I think that when we started to have the “likes” and then cascading comments, you’re suddenly in this kind of market-research environment where people can give you feedback. And I think that just the very fact of likes and comments kind of puts a person in a position to be like, Okay, well, now I’m looking for your approval. Now I want to see how—I want to do this because I want you guys to like it. So there’s that, just very simply, the interface kind of puts us in that position. I think if we didn’t have those features we would behave differently. And I think that’s true on interfaces where there aren’t these kinds of interactive features, people do behave differently. If you think about like Flickr or whatever, these photo-sharing sites, people just put photos and it’s different. We have been over the last 20 years in this period of precarity becoming a larger and larger part of the economic environment, the workplace environment. People are having to kind of try to promote themselves, even if they’re not really trying to sell anything. They are kind of like, I need to look my best. I want to try to maintain a certain reputation. You’re competing in the job market. You feel more and more that you’re competing in the social environment, like in the world of dating.

When I try to explain to the college students that I teach, There’s other ways of telling a story about yourself or presenting yourself to the world than this branded self where you’re trying to demonstrate a certain kind of fitness and you want to always look a certain way, they don’t understand what I mean at all. Because to them, it’s like, Why wouldn’t I want to have people think that I’m the best version of myself? That’s my purpose, is to get better and better at something, become a better version of myself, get more fit, whatever the case may be. I’m working on myself. I’m trying to get better. I want people to see that. I want people to see that I’m trying and that I’m succeeding. And they can’t comprehend that there’s a different narrative structure around selfhood that could possibly exist. And the fact is there was, before social media, that everyone lived in: that you were a person, you had your hobbies, you had your goals, you had your the things that you were up to, but your self might have been somewhat separate from this, these sets of work concerns or creative concerns. And it really wasn’t all one thing that you were trying to convince people of. I think that we accepted that there was something about each of us that was a little bit uncontainable or like, you know, just ourselves.

Warzel: Mm-hmm. Or worth protecting, yeah.

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, worth protecting. And I think that that idea has just completely faded into a kind of obsolescence.

Warzel: The precarity part is really fascinating to me, especially in the way that it is a behavior that obviously benefits the platforms. If you don’t post with a certain type of frequency now, it’s less at-bats, right? Less chances for the algorithm to reward you or to be seen, or to whatever, or to make money off of whatever thing, or have a brand deal. But it’s also just to exist, right? You disappear in these things if you don’t continue to feed them. There’s just too much to drown you out if you’re not also doing the constant connection and posting, and whether that’s in the dating space, or just on Instagram or Twitter sharing stories and articles—whatever it is, TikTok, you name it, YouTube.

Jezer-Morton: This is what happens, I think, when people go through a really difficult time. You’ll see they’ll disappear because they can’t narrate, like a divorce, illness, tragedy. Sometimes people will narrate through it. You’ll see that. And it’s very interesting. But a lot of the time, people don’t, because they’re like, I don’t know how to accommodate this complexity of feeling. I can’t narrate it. So I’m just out of here. And then if they want to come back, it’s like, then you have to make some kind of statement, like, Hey, I’m back. I think that this is where we hit the limitations of the medium. It doesn’t welcome us back in a way that feels full of possibility. It feels like you have to kind of engage within the constraints of this brand environment. And to me, I think it’s very inhibiting for people who are going through complex, deeply ambivalent life chapters. And so—and I say this in the book—we don’t have that many examples of telling stories that have to do with struggle and ambivalence and pain because people just don’t know how to do it. And so the longer we don’t do it, the longer we’re not going to do it because we just don’t have examples to look to like, Oh, well, that person narrated their really painful divorce in a way that really made sense to me. And so I can kind of build on that. You just don’t see these stories. You see people having bounced back.

Warzel: Well, this is what I wanted to go to next too, which is the idea of what you call “master narratives” in the, sort of, architecture a lot of these platforms build towards, right? One of them being things like redemption—redemption being a very important one of those, or just progress in general as a kind of master narrative. But what are some of the other master narratives that these platforms favor?

Jezer-Morton: I mean, I think redemption is the No. 1, which is just, you know, I’m getting better and better. I’m overcoming. I think just the idea of, even within suffering, battling an illness, overcoming, being a warrior—all of this kind of military sort of metaphors around illness and recovery.

I think that’s the main one. I think it’s to do with just being someone who is going to overcome it, gonna kill it, gonna be awesome in the end. And I think there are certainly exceptions to this rule. And I think especially among younger people, you’re seeing people talk about suffering in new ways to me, that I’m kind of impressed with. But I would say among Millennials and older people, even like a GoFundMe, for example—which, you know, a GoFundMe is about suffering. People don’t usually make their own GoFundMe pages. They’re made on behalf of someone. And you accept the charity of your friend who kindly sets up a GoFundMe on your behalf. People don’t do it for themselves. And I really do think that’s just like a bit of—it’s like a value system at work. People are like, I can’t. I don’t want to be seen asking for help. I want someone to ask for help for me. And I think that’s part of the same master narrative. Like, If I’m asking for help, I’m asking for pity. I’m asking for—it feels very wrong, very uncomfortable for most people to do that. Which is really interesting because asking for help is extremely human, and any therapist will tell you that it’s really good to do it. And it’s good to get comfortable doing it. But I think it’s something that people have a very hard time with.

Warzel: So with the idea of demonstrating growth or progress or redemption, you also say that social-media structure penalizes what you call “flat stories.” So what are flat stories?

Jezer-Morton: So a flat story is a story that doesn’t have an upward-trending arc. So it’s like, Yeah, I got a divorce and I’m not sure if it was a good idea or not. And honestly, I’m very confused, but life goes on. It’s like, I’m having a really hard time in this job, and I don’t feel like I’m doing a good job, but I’m gonna try to hang on for as long as possible because I need the money. Right?

And for me, the novel is the technology of the flat story. My favorite novels are novels that kind of end with this feeling where you’re like, Dang, you know, Oof. Life. Ain’t it just like that? You know, like The Age of Innocence by Edith Wharton, where he’s like, Yep, I’m just gonna be with someone who I’m not in love with. And as a reader, you’re like, Oh God, devastating. But like—and I think this is why people love novels—it puts you in someone else’s subject position, it introduces a whole other reality, and then it kind of forces you to account for how being a human is complex and hard. And, I mean, it’s the best, right?

So, okay, that’s novels. Social media: not the same thing. The technology affords different stories. And for me, like the way I started thinking about flat stories was the commune of my childhood. It’s still around; it’s been around for 50 years. There’s only a couple people living there now, but it keeps on somehow. But it’s not a triumphant story. Like, 100 percent, the golden age was in the past. But if you go up there, you’re like, Man, this place is kind of cool. This is different. These people are cool and getting old, and they’re here. And it’s hard to place it within a narrative framework that I think many of us are familiar with.

Warzel: What I can’t stop thinking about as you’re talking about this is the idea, similar to the commune, that so much of business pre–social media and the internet—like family businesses, right? Like, it’s the hardware store that just kind of is around for 75 years, and like, is it going well? Yeah, we have some good months and some good years, and then there’s some bad years. And yeah, we had to replace the roof and took out a loan, whatever. Versus the narrative around business, finance, the economy now, which is just like, it can’t be a flat narrative, right? In order to raise venture capital money to do whatever, it’s growth at all costs. It’s scale. “Number go up,” right? All these things just have to increase and increase and increase, and it’s better and better. And the story has to be algorithmically enticing. But just the way that this all bleeds into everything.

Now it’s a weird thing. You can find a way to post about, like, “My store endured,” right? “My hardware store endured forever.” But it’s not an interesting cultural narrative anymore to exist and to persist in that way. It has to be this growth. I think that’s really fascinating, that it seems to be bleeding in very much to just the general concept of what success is and can be.

Jezer-Morton: Exactly. No, it’s this idea that you have to 10X your story or you’re dead. It’s crazy that this has become kind of a narrative, any kind of concern that we have. But if you talk to a teenager—like, I have a 15-year-old son. He’s almost 16, and he doesn’t really use social media, but like a lot of teens, boys in particular—I don’t really know that much about what girls are up to, but—they’re into fitness. They go to the gym. That’s cool. Go to the gym, sure. What can I say? Fine. And he’s not taking supplements, but it’s just, it’s an activity that allows you to think in terms of getting better and better and better. It just has that built in. And so I don’t even know how much he likes going to the gym. I really can’t tell. But it allows him to participate in the discourse of I was here (Gestures lower.) and now I’m here (Gestures higher.), and in a year I’ll be here (Gestures even higher.).

And I think it’s like socially, especially if you’re young, it just makes sense. It’s easy. You plug yourself in, and now you have something to talk about with tons and tons of people. And I’m convinced it’s part of the same thing. Listen, human beings are interested in the body. It’s not like this is unprecedented. But I think that wherever you can get your growth narrative is where you’re gonna try to get it. And the gym is one such place. There’s a reason why optimization culture is what everyone is part of. It’s not just because we’re obsessed with being better. It’s because it’s a very convenient way of telling your story as a person in a way that other people can understand. And I really think that social media has given us all the training to participate in this.

Warzel: And it’s safe too, right? It’s very safe to be like, I’m just trying to get better, you know? Who’s gonna be like, Get rid of this guy?

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, what a loser. Yikes.

Warzel: He’s trying to be healthy. So okay, so we’ve established that social media teaches us to sell a story of ourselves as this product; that we’re locked into these master narratives improvement, redemption, resilience. And the algorithms then also reward the most legible, the most emotionally salient and intense versions of all of this.

Warzel: And then what you were right about in the book is how our lives start to reorganize themselves around this. And I’d love to kind of go through a couple of those examples. And the first one is vacations. So what have you learned from studying posts about vacations from influencers but also just from regular people?

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, so I went to Scottsdale, Arizona, and I hung out with some moms there. And this one mom said this amazing thing to me. She was like, Oh yeah, like when I’m posting, especially on trips, activities out and about with my family, I just want people to see that we do shit. We do shit. We are a family that does shit. We’re not boring, and we’re active, and we’re really good at making the best of it. We’re out in the world. And so I think a vacation is a great opportunity to kind of stage a really successful, kind of engaged, spirit of We know how to make the most of our time together. We’re not stuck inside. We’re not ruminating. We’re not grumping at each other. We’re at the Eiffel Tower; we’re grinning; we got here; we’re having the time of our lives. And so it creates this kind of affective container almost, like travel does, vacations do, and then just creating these really legible scenes around big landmarks that everyone recognizes—you know, like Positano, whatever it is, a place that everyone’s like, “Beautiful, yes, you made it.”

Vacations were not always an opportunity to show people your economic and emotional fitness. It used to be about other things too.

Warzel: Something that that you note, though, that I think is really interesting to this this broader idea is that it kind of makes us—because there’s these conventions in this in this way of doing something even that we’ve done forever, like vacations—there’s this small-c conservatism to it, right? Can you say a little more about how it pushes people to be more conservative, not ideologically or politically, but just in what they do?

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, so small-c conservatism, meaning just like the desire to replicate things as they have previously been done. Like tradition. It’s usually done like this, so I wanna do it that way. I want to replicate the photo that I’ve seen. And by doing it successfully, I will have succeeded. As opposed to like, for example, in other eras, people might have been like, When I go on vacation, I want to have a transcendent experience where I feel maybe like I’m transformed or like the place gets under my skin and I feel like a different version of myself altogether that I may take home with me or I may not. But it’s very, kind of, you could call it woo-woo, you can call it whatever you want, but it’s to do with the mysteries of the self. It has nothing to do with proving or re-creating anything that you’ve seen other people do. You’re like, No, I’m gonna do it in a completely new way, getting loose. So yeah, this conservatism has to do with like, I just want it to look the way that you know the pictures look when the influencers do it.

And I see this in a lot of young people. For them, the enjoyment of having gotten just the right shot, making something look really “aesthetic,” as they say, it’s a deep enjoyment for them. It’s a source of real satisfaction that I can’t relate to. I’m too old, but I see they’re like, Ooh, this, this is fun. We’re having fun now because we got just the right frame. We got everything in it just right.

Warzel: Yeah, and I think it’s important, what I notice in your work and in this conversation is not like belittling that, right? It’s not passing judgment on that, just noting that that has actually happened. I think it’s very similar with phones at concerts and things like that, where there are some people who see it and go, like, Great, so you’re not even doing the thing. You’re not even engaged with this, you’re just so consumed with capturing it. And you’ll hear a lot of people say, like, I’m having a great time. This is what I’m here to do. I’m here to capture this in this way.

Jezer-Morton: No, totally. And I say this in the book—and I would actually like to spend more time thinking about this because I didn’t really have time to develop it—I think that when people feel the emotion of, like, I’m having fun. This feels so great. Here we are at the concert. I think that taking out your phone and capturing it has now become part of expressing that emotion. Emotions are partly in our bodies, but they’re also partly culturally expressed, like people express emotions differently in other parts of the world. And I think that the taking out of the phone and being like, We’re gonna get this capture, it’s part and parcel of this feeling of like, This is so awesome. I am loving this. And I don’t think that it’s the same thing as, you know, erasing yourself from the moment or failing to experience it. I think it’s part of experiencing it for a lot of people.

Warzel: Let’s move into politics, specifically the way that the internet is shaping political identities. How have you seen social media changing the way that we express and perform our politics in this way?

Jezer-Morton: Fundamentally, we’re performing as brands. We are compelled to act this way, but in fact, being a person is a very terrible fit for branding. We’re constantly in violation of our own brand guidelines. We’re constantly failing to be consistent. That’s what being a person is. It’s a mess. It’s like square peg in a round hole, personal branding and being a person. And I think that really comes up, it shows in politics because I think we assume that when someone is posting about politics, they’re coming from a place of cool-headed, like I’m making a statement on the events, when often, and I found this in my research, it’s very emotional and it’s very irrational. And maybe there’s like a couple people out there in the audience that you’re trying to get through to, and you really don’t care what anyone else thinks, but these are the people that you’re in communication with—or whatever, you’re working through something, you’re compensating for something—whatever it is, you have ulterior motives and you’re expressing them through your posts, the things that you’re sharing about politics.

And I think it’s very easy to misinterpret that and to think that, you know, Oh, this person is just stating their political views, when in fact there’s so many other things going on.

Warzel: A corollary to the politics part of this is how the platforms, and all of our collective behaviors on the platforms, change our relationships to facts and truth. And you have an observation here that I think is—I spent a lot of time just thinking about it, so I’d love for you to explain this out even more for me, which is the idea that truth in some ways has been replaced by the idea of authenticity. Can you tease that out a little more for me and for everyone listening?

Jezer-Morton: Yeah. So authenticity being that someone is willing to kind of put themselves out there or seem really real, seem unfiltered, seem sort of unpracticed. And I think it is a little bit of a maybe we have a sort of a fatigue or we’re getting wary of the whole personal brand polish and we want people who kind of violate the rules of personal branding.

Donald Trump: perfect example, right? He’s not a very consistent persona. He does all kinds of stuff that is very contradictory. And for that reason, he’s considered very authentic. Like, He says what he means, even if it contradicts what he just said. You always know that he’s coming from someplace that is real within him, or whatever. I mean, authentic doesn’t mean “true” anymore. It has a different meaning.

And I think we see this—so the example that I gave, and I see so many examples of this now all over Instagram, is: No one’s interested in scientific data as much as they’re interested in a really compelling anecdote. And this is just attention-economy stuff. This is because a really compelling anecdote is going to perform better for a number of reasons, whereas a big, longitudinal study is gonna have some interesting findings but it’s also gonna have some contradictory findings, or it’s not always gonna—science is often much less explosive than this one dude who’s like, I took this supplement, and six months later I am freaking jacked. You know, that’s cool. I can see the results. These charts, like, Ugh, it involved like 50,000 people, subjects—there’s some real conclusive evidence here, but it’s way less fun. The results are just much more ambiguous.

We’re living in the age of the anecdote. The anecdote is so much better than the data. Because the anecdote comes from someone’s passion. It involves this affective kind of loadedness that we get to appreciate.

Warzel: I’ve talked about this with certain influencers before, and it’s so interesting because in my professional career, like we’re here at The Atlantic, this is an institution that’s been around for a long time. There’s a lot of credibility that is supposed to come with that and through the processes of, whether it’s The Atlantic or The New York Times or any media institution or any university or place that has been around and has norms and standards and has built up a trust around that. And what you see in the current attention economy, as you say, is the truth being replaced by the authentic-feeling anecdote. But also too is the feeling of, with the authenticity that comes from the influencer and not the institution, is the forgiveness that comes from that, right? Like, an influencer screws up and it’s like, Hey man, it’s just one guy. He’s out, she’s out there. They’re just hustling. They’re making a million videos. They’re posting all the time. What do you expect? They’re gonna get some stuff wrong, man. But they’re trying, and they’re real, and they’re not corporate. Versus, you know, The New York Times or The Washington Post or The Atlantic or whoever makes a mistake, and it’s like, no forgiveness.

Jezer-Morton: Yeah. How dare you?

Warzel: Yeah, the person who feels authentic is given so much rope in these situations.

Jezer-Morton: Yeah, I think that when someone is like, I’m gonna stream my life, and I’m gonna show you my whole my whole vibe, people are like, I honestly don’t care what they say. I love that they’re showing me their whole vibe. And I think that people—again, I think this is maybe a little bit of a response to a fatigue of this kind of perfect brand itself—people are like, No, I want to watch someone just be in front of the camera for eight hours talking about any old thing, and I’ll listen to them, and I’m into it because it feels really real. I’ll listen to their anecdotes. I’ll just catch their vibe. And it feels satisfying in a way that, you know, when people are pretending to be perfect, we’re losing maybe some of the satisfaction of that.

Warzel: I wanna zoom out a little because you argue that stories—humans are storytellers—historically expand our understanding of human beings, who we are, what we can do, and they invite really big open-ended questions, but that social media and its stories are kind of shrinking. Instead of the open-ended questions, it’s like the aperture is narrower.

Is social media and these platforms that we’re telling our stories on, are they shrinking our idea of what the world can be?

Jezer-Morton: I think so. I think we’re always trying to fit our experience into these very limiting narratives that social media gives us. And I think that has an effect of shrinking our capacity. And I do think that ultimately so much of human life, it’s an imaginative activity. Like everyone’s talking about The Odyssey right now. The Odyssey before it was written down was many, many versions of the same story that had many possible endings. And people who heard the story of Odysseus had heard it told in a number of different ways. And they accepted the fact that this story had infinite possible endings. And that was cognitively normal for them. They were like: a given story, who knows how it’s gonna end? And I do think that that gives people a capacity to understand life in a different way than people who are mostly hearing their narratives from social media, or they’re really just hearing about how people are doing awesome and they’re growing and they’re improving and they’re overcoming. And it feels pretty unidirectional and it just feels limited. And I just think that the stories that you hear help you to then tell your own story. And the stories that we hear are not as capacious as they could be.

Warzel: Well, and I think there’s something too of the relentless growth and resilience and positivity as the master narratives, as you call them, as they sandwich up against the reality, the precarity that we also talked about that you’re experiencing, right, when you’re looking at whether it’s climate change or economic insecurity or “AI’s coming for whatever” or political unrest.

You see all that and it’s like, No, but the story has to be this way, and it’s hard to reckon the two of them. And I think that kind of makes a person feel a little insane.

You wrote something I felt very, very deeply, as a fellow person who’s spent the last two decades on social media, and I’m gonna quote you to yourself here: “It is humiliating to try to account for our experiences on platforms that are obviously hostile towards their users. It’s degrading. We’re being treated like shit, and not surprisingly, it’s getting to us. After enough years of this degradation, we may start to believe we are shit. Is it any surprise that contempt and self-loathing animates so much of what’s left of posting culture?”

And personally, I feel like less and less attached to the story of myself as a result of all this, the story I’m telling on these platforms. It is work now. It’s not fun. It’s begun to feel like work. And without a viable alternative—we’re probably not gonna get off these platforms or just have a wholesale change of our behaviors—but I do wonder if you think there’s gonna be something of a wake-up. Like we’ll stop posting on the platforms as terms, maybe, or that we’ll begin to treat them very differently and almost in a kind of protest to what they want us to be. Do you see that happening, or do you think that it’s just so entwined with our lives and identities that we’re just gonna continue to be living in this abusive relationship?

Jezer-Morton: I really see this book as like my farewell to the posting era. I do think that people are posting less. I think they’re going to be posting less and less. I think more social media is going to be populated by AI anyway. And I think the humans are going to have less and less of a role to play. And I do think we’re going to come up with something different. It’s not going to be like a new social-media platform. I don’t believe that that’s imminent. But I think we do come up with creative solutions. We have workarounds. We do find a way to kind of escape capture in our storytelling. We manage that. Memes are one such way, I think. I don’t know about a wake-up call. That feels a little major. I think it’s gonna be slow. I think it’s gonna be very gradual. But I think that people already are like, This narrative tool is no longer working for me. And I don’t know what we’re gonna replace it with, but I know that the desire, the need to tell our stories to each other and to ourselves is gonna find a new container somehow. I fully believe that.

Warzel: I hope that it is something that is not owned by Mark Zuckerberg, whatever it is.

Jezer-Morton: Me too.

Warzel: Kathryn, thank you so much for coming on Galaxy Brain and and talking through these perfectly galaxy-brained concepts with us.

Jezer-Morton: Thanks so much for having me.

Warzel: That’s it for us here. Thank you to my guest, Kathryn Jezer-Morton. Just a quick show note: We are going on a little bit of a hiatus for a portion of this summer to spend some time thinking about what we’re going to do for the new episodes. But we will be back very soon, I promise you that.

And if you want to support this work and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. And as a little Easter egg for all of those of you who have made it here through the credits: You may have noticed something wispy and strange behind me. I lost a bet to a bunch of my friends on a golf trip and had to get a mullet. So if you stuck around, this one’s for you. Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet.

entries.content:
Today The Atlantic is announcing two new staff writers: Madeleine Carlisle and Danyel Smith. This marks a homecoming for Madeleine, who was an Atlantic editorial fellow in 2018 and 2019, and went on to Time magazine and most recently 60 Minutes. Danyel is a legend in journalism who spent the past three years as a contributing writer to The New York Times Magazine and was previously the editor of both Vibe and Billboard.

Below is the staff announcement from editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg:

Dear everyone,

I’m very happy to let you know that two extraordinary journalists are joining The Atlantic as staff writers: Madeleine Carlisle and Danyel Smith. Both names should be familiar to you; Danyel’s because she is a legend in journalism, having served as the editor in chief of both Vibe and Billboard; and Maddie’s because she is one of our profession’s rising stars (and in particular because she jump-started her journalism career in 2018 as an Atlantic fellow).



About Danyel, who is coming to us from The New York Times Magazine: I’ve been reading Danyel for years, starting, if memory serves, with her brilliant, definitive 1995 cover profile of Whitney Houston, and continuing on through her piercingly forthright 2024 feature in the Times, “I Knew Diddy for Years. What I Now Remember Haunts Me.”



Danyel is a brilliant observer of popular culture—and of the music world in particular—who will bring deep knowledge to our reporting and criticism. Danyel’s list of achievements is long. In addition to leading both Vibe and Billboard, she has been an editor and writer at ESPN and is the author of Shine Bright: A Very Personal History of Black Women in Pop. Danyel has profiled some of the biggest names in pop culture (Lionel Richie, Tina Turner, Barry Manilow, SZA), and she will do more of this for us.

About Maddie: A bunch of us sensed that, sooner or later, she would be coming back to us. Maddie was a very successful member of the 2018–19 fellowship class who went on to cover politics, law, and gender issues for Time magazine. She then joined the 60 Minutes team, where she worked with correspondents Scott Pelley, Anderson Cooper, and Cecilia Vega on their stories, including one about crypto billionaire Changpeng Zhao that earned an Emmy nomination for outstanding investigative coverage.

As a fellow on the Politics team, she wrote about a Florida woman whose nephew was killed in the Parkland shooting, and about President Trump’s unfulfilled promises to GM workers in Ohio. We’ve been so happy to watch her become an outstanding journalist, and we’re thrilled that she’s rejoining The Atlantic.

Please join me in welcoming both Maddie and Danyel.

Best wishes,

Jeff

entries.title: A Chatbot-Free Childhood Will Be a Status Symbol
entries.summary: AI is like ultra-processed food for developing brains.
entries.content:
AI is like ultra-processed food for developing brains.

The human brain has evolved to learn from specific instructors. When a child hears a gentle spoken word or a soothing lullaby from another person, when their cry is responded to, their brain lights up. Nurturing interactions, or what child-development experts call “serve and return” exchanges, help shape and strengthen the 1 million new neural connections taking place in a child’s brain every single second. Every time a child cries or serves up a bid for attention and receives a caregiver’s response, that back-and-forth helps build the circuits underlying their communication, learning, and emotional well-being. No other input, not even Johann Pachelbel’s Canon in D performed by the Berlin Philharmonic, is capable of activating the neural circuitry the way human interaction does.

Until now. Generative AI may be the first technology in history sophisticated enough to mimic the social interactions that build our brains. Research has demonstrated that infants as young as six months old respond physiologically to interactions with humanoid robots in ways that mirror their response to live humans; another, small-scale experimental study recently found that, after young children interacted with a chatbot, most of them for the first time, they asserted that the AI could perceive the world with humanlike senses and understand and learn as people do.

This technology is already showing up in children’s lives. The talking plush robot that purports to be a child’s best friend is obviously driven by AI, but many parents may not realize that their Amazon Echo recently received a software update that converts the Alexa voice assistant into a full-blown chatbot, using the same fundamental tech that fuels ChatGPT; toddlers asking for information about animals or a joke or a bedtime story may quickly find themselves in the habit of engaging socially with a large language model.

As a pediatric surgeon, researcher, and technologist who has spent decades studying how children’s brains develop, I am concerned about these technologies rolling out and being used by children in the home and at school before we have a full sense of their safety and what they do to young minds. And I am compelled to point out what we do know about human development: that human connection, in all of its imperfection, is foundational to brain development. It can’t be engineered or recovered later.

When a disruption as significant as the AI revolution occurs, people might look for a comparison to make sense of the transformation. In this case, many people instinctively think of social media. After all, it, too, amounted to a large-scale technological experiment that produced unexpected problems that we are still attempting to fully comprehend. But even that comparison is insufficient, because interactive AI—and its ability to mimic the serve-and-return exchanges that wire developing brains—is utterly, fundamentally different from every consumer technology that came before it.

During the most foundational period of brain development, social interaction of the sort that AI can now emulate isn’t entertainment for the developing brain. It’s nutrition. Once you see it that way, the right parallel snaps into focus. A more apt comparison than social media is food—more precisely, processed food.

For a long time, no one needed to specify that food was farm-raised. The alternative didn’t exist. Food was grown on farms and in gardens and was prepared in homes and in kitchens. But in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, that changed. Food production was industrialized, transformed by genuinely beneficial innovations such as canning, refrigeration, preservation, and mass distribution. Real and urgent problems were addressed: Growing cities were fed, harsh winters became less lethal, life expectancy increased, and kids grew taller and lived longer.

But in the early days, food manufacturers were conducting their own uncontrolled experiments. Preservatives and additives flooded the food supply as companies adopted solutions that they promised were safe: morphine in cough syrup, chalk in milk, formaldehyde in meat. A government chemist, Harvey Washington Wiley, recognized that these evidence-free innovations posed a threat to public health. To prove this, Wiley recruited a cadre of young men willing to eat meals laced with those very preservatives while scientists observed the effects. The suffering of this so-called Poison Squad helped spark the Pure Food and Drug Act of 1906.

We’re in a modern Wiley moment. Innovations in artificial intelligence are delivering very real benefits to today’s families: diagnostic aids that catch developmental delays earlier than human screeners likely can, real-time translation tools that allow non-English-speaking immigrant parents to engage with their children’s teachers, productivity apps that reduce the administrative burdens weighing down many parents and educators. But these innovations have also unleashed obvious dangers: teddy bears that describe sexual kinks or teach toddlers to light matches, AI-generated videos that highlight made-up letters and words.

Despite these dramatic examples of AI gone wrong, the real danger—as demonstrated by our food supply—is what happens when these systems work exactly as designed.

By the mid-20th century, food companies had discovered something more profitable than feeding people: engineering the desire to keep eating. They hired scientists—chemists, flavor engineers, behavioral researchers—to find the precise formulas that would override the body’s natural signal that said “enough.” They discovered the “bliss point”—the precise combination of sugar, fat, and salt that maximizes pleasure in the human brain—and engineered foods to hit this target. They began producing what is now often called ultra-processed food.

This new food looked like its more natural predecessors. It came in familiar shapes. It sat on the same shelves. But something fundamental had changed. Although some ambiguities and controversies surround what foods fall into the broad term ultra-processed—in some respects, it’s a fancy way of saying “junk food”—many of these items are filled with additives and are engineered to be easy to eat and digest in large quantities. They may use hyper-palatable combinations that have been engineered to light up our brain’s reward systems. How could natural foods compete with that?

In short: They couldn’t. Whole foods slowly disappeared from our diet. Today, the average American receives 55 percent of their daily calories from ultra-processed foods—items that didn’t even exist a century ago. For children ages 1 to 18, the number is close to 62 percent. The amount of calories that adults consumed from whole foods decreased from 32.7 to 27.4 percent from 2001 to 2018, according to the CDC’s National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. According to a 2021 CDC analysis, nearly a third of American children ages 1 to 5 didn’t eat fruit daily, and nearly half didn’t eat vegetables daily. More than half drank sugar-sweetened beverages weekly.

Food companies developed truly remarkable innovations to solve very real challenges. But with those innovations in hand, they also set out to grow revenue. The same market logic is now being applied to our interaction with tech. The underlying capabilities of AI are remarkable, but they can also be formulated to optimize for engagement.

At a glance, a child talking to an AI companion looks like a child participating in conversation. But essential, quiet interactions have been stripped away. Imperfections, delays, and the need to apologize or rephrase something may seem like flaws in human communication, but they are, in fact, crucial developmental building blocks. The small cycle of rupture and repair that occurs following a misunderstanding, played out thousands of times over a childhood, is how resilience, flexibility, and emotional regulation get built. It’s how children develop the most important relational skills: trusting that relationships can survive conflict, and staying connected with others through discomfort.

Remove the friction from childhood, and the social-emotional system never gets what it needs to properly develop. The neural architecture that was supposed to be built through imperfect, sometimes-frustrating human interaction may never fully form. Neither may frustration tolerance, empathy, or resilience. Cognitive skills may suffer too. Developmental scientists have long understood that children learn and grow by encountering tasks just beyond their current ability. This is called the “zone of proximal development,” and AI systems designed to meet a child exactly where they are risk denying them the opportunity to ever reach that zone.

Because AI companions have been engineered to remove every imperfection—the misunderstanding, the delay, the repair—a child’s social-emotional system never has to work. Ultra-processed foods stripped the fiber from diets, and engagement-optimized AI might strip the friction from childhood. The developing mind, like the gut, needs resistance to grow. Friction isn’t an obstacle to development; it is development.

Not everyone will be equally affected by the rollout of this new technology. People who have very low food security consume roughly 3 percent more ultra-processed food than those who have high food security do, in part because the cost for each calorie of unprocessed foods is more than 2.5 times that of ultra-processed foods. However, high-income families began pivoting away from ultra-processed foods as soon as the potential harms of such foods became apparent. “Clean” ingredients, minimally processed foods, and organic produce became available—and affordable—to those with resources. An “organic” diet became a status symbol.

An identical pattern is emerging with AI. Many of the engineers and executives building these products are going screen-free at home and doubling down on unstructured play. Jack Clark, a co-founder of Anthropic, told Ezra Klein earlier this year that the idea of his young daughter having “unfettered” access to the YouTube algorithm “freaks me out.” He added, “I have the classic Californian-technology-executive view of not having that much technology around for children.”

If the food parallel holds, then engagement-optimized AI will become the new Dollar Menu, concentrating in the lives of the children who can least afford its developmental cost. The Pew Research Center has already demonstrated through survey data that teens in lower-income households are more likely than those from higher-income homes to rely on chatbots for homework help.

We don’t yet have a large-scale study of children raised on ultra-processed interaction. That research is still decades away. But what keeps me up at night is the possibility that we’ll allow human connection to become the new organic—cherished and protected by the wealthy, and out of reach for everyone else.

This article has been adapted from Dana Suskind’s new book, Human Raised: Nurturing Connection, Curiosity & Lifelong Learning in the Age of AI.
