entries.title: The Most Basic Step of the Ebola Response Is Falling Short
entries.summary: Curbing the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo will require stepping up testing.
entries.content:
Curbing the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo will require stepping up testing.

The fight against Ebola is not going well. Last week, the head of Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya, announced that the ongoing outbreak of the virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo had ballooned into the second worst of all time, a milestone he had thought was possible to avoid only weeks before. Rather than the spread of the virus slowing, cases are doubling about every 10 days; more than 1,800 people have died, though the actual toll is likely at least twice as high. His organization is now fighting to keep this Ebola outbreak from becoming the worst on record, Kaseya said at a press conference.

This outbreak is spreading more quickly than any other in history partly because one of the basic tools needed to control infectious disease—testing for the pathogen—is not working. So the Congolese government, along with scientists, aid groups, the World Health Organization, and the world’s biotech companies, is racing to fix it.

In its early stages, Ebola can resemble several more common viruses, including malaria, so health-care workers rely on tests, rather than symptoms, to diagnose the disease. After the 2014 West African Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, Congo began stockpiling machines that could detect the Zaire species of Ebola virus, which causes most outbreaks. Hundreds of these GeneXpert devices are now in hospitals all over Congo, along with cartridges that can test a patient’s sample for the virus within an hour, Christian Happi, a molecular biologist who leads a team in Congo working on surveilling this outbreak, told me.

Health officials in Congo began using those stockpiles to test patients for Ebola on April 30, after a smattering of health-care-worker deaths, a calling card of the virus. The results came back negative. So did more samples a couple of weeks later. Ebola, we now know, was circulating. But the species turned out to be Bundibugyo, which is far rarer than Zaire, and which cannot be detected by the existing supply of GeneXpert cartridges. That didn’t become clear until officials had sent samples more than 1,000 miles away, to Kinshasa, for more robust PCR testing, creating a disastrous four-week gap between when the first known patient developed symptoms and when officials received laboratory confirmation of a new Ebola outbreak.

PCR testing is still the only reliable way to detect the Bundibugyo strain in Congo. Under the current system, a car drives to Ebola-treatment centers in affected regions, picks up tests, then drives back to labs that can run the tests, Trish Newport, a lead on Doctors Without Borders’ Ebola programs, explained to me. Some routes take longer than they otherwise would because the samples have to be driven over uneven roads that are frequently blocked by fighting between the Congolese military and the armed group known as M23. After the PCR is run, the car returns handwritten results to the centers.

Nineteen laboratories in Congo can now run PCR tests to detect Bundibugyo, which is a major improvement since the beginning of the outbreak, when only two labs had that capacity in a country of more than 116 million people. But according to figures released by Africa CDC in July, one in eight Ebola tests still took more than 72 hours to return a result. Despite the increase in Ebola testing, the proportion of tests that come back positive has stayed constant, about 45 percent. That probably means the country is still dramatically undertesting, Abraar Karan, an epidemiologist at Stanford, told me.

Meanwhile, Ebola is expanding into new parts of the country. Bringing the outbreak to heel will almost certainly require upping testing to catch more cases, trace chains of transmission, and isolate people who are contagious before they spread the disease further. Modeling done after the 2014 Ebola outbreak suggested that diagnosing 60 percent of patients within one day rather than within five days could have drastically reduced the infection rate.

The fastest solution to Congo’s testing crisis would be to distribute GeneXpert cartridges that can detect Bundibugyo. After all, hundreds of hospitals already have the machines, and each can run 80 or so patient samples at once, which would allow many patients to get same-day results, Happi said. A GeneXpert cartridge that tests for every human strain of Ebola does exist: The U.S. Department of Defense funded its development as part of a biothreat-preparedness program in 2020. The FDA approved the panel earlier this year—but only for use by labs at DOD, which intended to continue conducting research on them. (The Department of Defense did not respond to repeated requests for comment.)

In June, with DOD’s permission, Cepheid, the company that makes GeneXpert machines, donated at least some of the tests meant for U.S. government research to Congo’s national health system, Larry Kelmar, the vice president of government relations for Cepheid, told me. (Kelmar did not say how many.) But before they can be used, their accuracy will still need to be compared with PCR tests. Shanelle Hall, a principal adviser at Africa CDC, told me that the GeneXpert cartridges have been tested and that data from those tests are currently being analyzed. A decision on approval is expected in a matter of “weeks, maybe days.”

Other companies and institutions are scrambling to speed up testing, too. Last month, the Gates Foundation issued a Global Grand Challenge to fund teams that will work urgently to develop “field-ready” diagnostics. The WHO has selected eight Ebola diagnostics capable of detecting Bundibugyo—including the GeneXpert cartridges—for fast-track testing, and has already approved two. A test made by a South Korean company, the RADIONE, was approved for use in patients earlier this summer and has become the cornerstone of the WHO’s plan to decentralize and speed up Ebola testing. A senior official at Africa CDC told reporters in early June that 50 RADIONE machines would be in Congo by the end of that month. As of this week, 37 have been delivered. But the machines can test only 24 or so patient blood samples at once, too few to make the dent in diagnosis times needed, Happi said. In a statement, a spokesperson from the WHO said the organization has “established a joint validation platform to rapidly evaluate the performance of a selection of diagnostic products” and that the introduction of new PCR machines has increased testing capacity from 200 tests a day to more than 2,000. KH Medical, the small manufacturer that makes the RADIONE tests, did not respond to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, Happi told me, some Ebola-treatment centers without enough isolation wards are sending suspected Ebola patients home to wait for test results and, potentially, expose other people during that wait. Africa CDC also plans to intensify its contract-tracing efforts by sending thousands of health workers door-to-door, which would require still more testing capacity to support.

The wait for results can discourage the feverish from presenting themselves for testing, Newport, who has been in Congo most of this summer, said. In part because of the delays—and in part because many people in Congo are skeptical of international responders, or believe that treatment centers are places people go to die—those who show up to the hospital typically do so late in disease progression. That’s a real problem, not just because they stay in the community infectious for longer, but also because Ebola cases are far more survivable when they’re caught early, Newport said. Currently, most Ebola deaths are happening at home, rather than in a treatment center or hospital, meaning that many of these infections are never recorded and that teams meant to disinfect homes and sanitarily bury the dead to prevent further spread of the disease never intervene.

The shortage of tests throughout this outbreak has resulted in a shortage of answers to fundamental questions about how the disease has been spreading. Experts still disagree on whether the outbreak began in January or in April. Patient zero remains a mystery. Currently, 80 percent of people who test positive for Ebola haven’t had contact with any other confirmed patients. If that number doesn’t go down, Kaseya told reporters last week, “we will not stop this outbreak.”

entries.title: MAGA’s Most Famous Prisoner Is Free
entries.summary: Newly out of prison, Tina Peters is back to trying to prove election fraud.
entries.content:
Newly out of prison, Tina Peters is back to trying to prove election fraud.

This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here.

Earlier this year, Tina Peters was languishing in a Colorado women’s prison, eating processed food, and complaining of declining health—including a persistent cough, digestive issues, and bumps on her skin. But by the end of June, the woman who was convicted on charges tied to tampering with voting equipment under her control in 2020 strolled into the White House, sporting a tailored pinstripe suit and red lipstick, her hair cut in a sharp bob. She feasted on a fried-chicken-and-noodle dish with President Trump in his private dining room and posed for photos in the Oval Office. She told the president about her ordeal and “what prison does to a person,” and they both bemoaned the state of the nation’s voting systems. “He was kind. He listened,” Peters told me in an email.

Peters, once a martyr to the MAGA cause, is now a free woman, feted by the stolen-election movement. The former clerk and recorder of Mesa County, Colorado, was convicted in 2024 and sentenced to nearly nine years in prison after prosecutors said she deceived colleagues to grant an unauthorized person access to voting equipment. After returning to office, Trump, aided by his White House counsel and Justice Department, spearheaded a campaign to “Free Tina Peters” as MAGA commentators and her attorneys relentlessly used the power of their keyboards to demand her release. But because Peters was convicted of state charges, the only person with the power to get her out was Colorado Governor Jared Polis. The Democrat bowed to extraordinary pressure in May and granted Peters clemency despite pleas from prosecutors, his clemency board, and election officials that her punishment was just.

Peters was released on June 1 after serving about 20 months of her sentence. Her freedom came as Trump ordered the nation’s intelligence community to find proof of foreign interference in the 2020 presidential election—only for it to again come up empty. That hasn’t stopped Peters, who wants the government to go even further in its efforts to find fraud she alleges exists from 2020 and overhaul rules and systems over the next three months to prevent malfeasance in November’s midterm elections.

She walked out of prison repeating many of the unsubstantiated claims that helped land her behind bars. She immediately hit the MAGA circuit, appearing on podcasts and livestreams from locations that look straight out of Architectural Digest. She has crusaded against the machinery used to conduct American elections, insisting that votes have been flipped and that foreign adversaries could exploit future contests. She rails against prison conditions and calls for one of her critics—Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat—to be locked up. Her comeback tour has taken her around the country, including, on June 30, to the White House’s Presidential Walk of Fame, where a photo showed her glancing adoringly at Trump’s portrait while holding what appeared to be a Birkin bag. During the visit she and Trump talked about “election integrity,” Peters told me, including “why people need a process they can verify—paper, open counts, accountability.”

Peters has said in nearly all of these media appearances that the actions that landed her in prison were an attempt to expose irregularities in her county’s voting equipment. She insists that her incarceration was “retribution” for showing that votes could be flipped—though there is no evidence of that claim. Ahead of the midterms she is imploring Trump to declare a national emergency on elections as a way to try to assert federal control over contests that are, by constitutional design, run by state and local governments. “We don’t have to prove anymore that these machines are cheating, that the ballots are being harvested,” Peters told War Room, a show hosted by the Trump ally Steve Bannon. The chyron identified her as a Former Political Prisoner.

No longer subjected to rigid routines, head counts, or fixed mealtimes, Peters has enjoyed choosing her own food again, including steak, salads, and juicy tomatoes (“things that taste like they came from a kitchen instead of a tray.”) “Right now I’m trying to get healthy,” Peters told me. “See the people I love, and keep doing lawful work. I’m not interested in living bitter.” Her faith helped her endure especially tough moments. “I’m grateful to God,” she wrote. “Some days feel normal. Some don’t.” Peters must get permission from a parole officer before traveling out of state.

Election denial has become her full-time job. She directs supporters to her recently revamped website, where she asks that they contribute to her cause (a red “Donate” button hovers in the top-right corner). At a “Fraud Fighter Summit” off the Las Vegas Strip in June, Peters took the stage, clutching a bouquet of flowers, to the delight of the crowd, and a moderator gushed about how “wonderful” she looked. Peters talked on speakerphone with Roseanne Barr, who had planned to attend the conference but had to scrap her trip. “Congratulations for being released from detainment in a communist country, Tina,” the sitcom star said. “You are our hero.” They pledged to take a girls’ trip at some point soon. Hawaii, Peters said, sounded like a good destination, adding: “I can still travel.”

Peters has a history of finding herself embroiled in election disputes. She was elected Mesa County clerk and recorder in 2018 after campaigning on a promise to reopen a closed DMV office. Fruita, Colorado, got its motor-vehicles branch back, but Peters soon found herself in the middle of her first voting-related controversy. Nearly 600 ballots cast in a November 2019 election were found in a drop box outside the clerk’s office months later; an effort to recall Peters over the discovery failed to collect enough signatures. In November 2020 Trump won Mesa County, amassing nearly two-thirds of votes cast.

But that election, Peters claimed in 2021, was tainted. Prosecutors said that Peters ordered video cameras to be turned off and deceived colleagues to obtain credentials that allowed an election-denial activist to access election equipment. Peters ran for Colorado secretary of state, despite being charged with numerous felonies, on a platform that included the claim that election equipment posed a threat to democracy. She lost in the primary. In 2024, a jury found her guilty of seven charges, including four felonies. The judge presiding over the case called Peters a “charlatan” and said that Peters, not faulty equipment, posed a threat to the electoral process.

Trump returned to the Oval Office a few months after her conviction and quickly started a campaign to spring her from prison through pressure and threats of retaliation. He warned that “harsh measures” would ensue if she remained incarcerated and directed his Justice Department “to take all necessary action to help secure the release of this ‘hostage.’” Peters was convicted on state charges beyond Trump’s pardon power, but in December he issued one anyway. Senior U.S. District Court Judge R. Brooke Jackson, in a preliminary order blocking the administration’s threat to cut Colorado’s SNAP benefits, noted in March that Trump called Polis “weak and pathetic” for keeping Peters confined, and that the administration had launched “a barrage of threats and actions designed, by all appearances, to punish Colorado.” They included terminating millions of Department of Transportation funds, threatening cancellation of energy funds, announcing a plan to dismantle the Boulder-based National Center for Atmospheric Research, and denying federal disaster-relief assistance.

An appeals court upheld Peters’s conviction a few weeks later, but found that the judge who presided over her case may have improperly considered her public comments—violating her First Amendment rights—and ordered that she be resentenced. Instead, Polis decided to commute her sentence. He wrote that hers was an “extremely unusual and lengthy sentence for a first time offender who committed nonviolent crimes.” An addendum to her clemency application that I obtained shows she acknowledges having “made mistakes,” that she pledged to obey the law if released, and that she noted that she wouldn’t have the ability to commit similar crimes since she is no longer a county clerk. “My work to ensure honest elections,” she wrote, “will continue.”

When Peters was freed, on June 1, Francis McClelland was ready to greet her. Carrying a handmade sign reading Tina Peters Mahalo for Your Sacrifice Fight Fight Fight, the 69-year-old stood outside of the La Vista Correctional Facility in Pueblo with a handful of other supporters. McClelland had never understood why Peters would be imprisoned for trying to help prove that elections are rigged, and so he rented a car in Philadelphia and drove out to Colorado hoping to see her. But he made the trip in vain. Neither state-prison officials nor those close to her would say where she was, citing security concerns. “I just wanted to be in the area and if she saw the sign, just to know that, ‘Hey, man, you made a sacrifice,’” McClelland, an independent Trump supporter from Hawaii, told me. “You shouldn’t back down when you’re right,” he said. “I do believe she’s right.”

Peters told me her early days outside of prison were mostly quiet, and devoted to the simple pleasures of her new freedom. She slept, and ate avocados. She went outside without asking permission. “I called people,” she told me. “I hugged people. I did boring grown-up stuff you can’t do inside. It wasn’t a parade. It was me trying to feel like a person.”

In her first media appearance after her release, on War Room, Peters appeared alongside a friend and looked tired. “I feel like I’ve aged about 10 years,” she said. She called her release a “miracle” and thanked Trump, her attorneys, and the supporters who sent money through her website. She said she had a long road to clear her name and then went right back to the themes that had landed her in trouble, saying that Democrats “are going to cheat” in elections. “No one’s really addressing the problem that I spent my time in prison as retribution for,” she said. “And that was exposing the election machines that allow the votes to be flipped. As we’re coming up to our 250-year anniversary, I’m joyful that we still have our liberty but, at the same time, I’m very concerned and burdened with why no one is talking about this.”

The Tina Peters tour hasn’t stopped since. She joins the MAGA-sphere from a constantly changing rotation of tastefully decorated settings, including a room with small duck figurines in the background and another with furniture upholstered in black-and-white chevron. She was spotted at a gathering with Arizona’s Kari Lake, another prominent voice in the election-skeptic movement. And wherever she appears, she always implores viewers to hit that red “Donate” button on her site.

In June, a 12-hour online “Lift Tina Telethon” featured a roster of MAGA personalities applauding her sacrifice. She was likened to Joan of Arc and Nelson Mandela, and someone suggested that her face should be carved into Mount Rushmore. A banner crawling across the bottom of the screen asked viewers to Please DONATE NOW to reach a fundraising goal that one speaker set from $1 million to $2 million. Peters made her appearance midway through, and choked up almost immediately. She spoke of her time in prison, during which she wrote letters to Trump, and of a call she had with the president after her release. “I told him, ‘I only wrote two people while I was in prison,’” she said. “I got thousands and thousands of letters. I’m just so humbled and grateful because you guys were, and still are, the wind beneath my wings.” Peters said she told Trump she was discouraged that little progress had been made to secure election equipment. She hoped to talk more about it with him soon. She was staring down other problems, the kind that viewer donations might fix: Her air-conditioning had gone out, and so had the brakes on her truck. “It’s real difficult for me to ask for myself,” she said.

The tour’s biggest stop, the White House, came at Trump’s request, according to Peters’s attorney Peter Ticktin. “He really admires her because she’s an American hero—and he referred to her as such,” Ticktin, a longtime friend of the president’s, told me. “She’s the one he wanted to meet.” Ticktin declined to say what was discussed. Peters said she felt valued during that visit. She spoke with the president about what she saw as a county clerk, how prison affects people, and of the need for “paper, open counts, accountability” in elections. “He talked like he actually cares what happens to regular people,” she wrote to me, “which is not how a lot of papers write him up.” At one point during the visit, she clutched a red AMERICA IS BACK! hat. She also met with Ed Martin, the U.S. pardon attorney, and was presented with a gold eagle brooch representing the Eagle Forum, the conservative advocacy group founded by Phyllis Schlafly.

The White House spokesperson Abigail Jackson did not answer questions about the meeting with Peters, but said in a statement that “President Trump is committed to ensuring that Americans have full confidence in the administration of elections, and that includes totally accurate and up-to-date voter rolls free of errors and unlawfully registered non-citizen voters.” Trump wants Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship and voter ID to vote, as well as “other legislative proposals that would establish a uniform standard of photo ID for voting, prohibit no-excuse mail-in voting, and end the practice of ballot harvesting,” Jackson wrote.

Two weeks after Peters visited the White House, Trump delivered a primetime address on election security, but again failed to provide clear evidence of fraud in the 2020 election. Many, including Peters, had hoped for more. On X, she called on Trump to “declare a National emergency” surrounding elections “to protect our country.” She later joined a handful of other election activists calling on federal officials to enforce a “Risk Mitigation Election Plan” before November that would, among other things, require hand-counting each ballot for federal contests before votes are certified, and compare them with counts tallied by electronic tabulators. “The objective is clear: reduce the opportunity for cheating,” read a July 24 letter from the activists to the acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. CISA did not answer my questions about the activists’ proposed plan or a meeting the activists said they had with the agency.

Many of the people who administer America’s elections are dismayed by Peters’s post-prison celebrity. Her efforts to convince people that their elections can’t be trusted make the job of administrators more difficult and dangerous, they told me. “She didn’t learn a thing,” Carly Koppes, the Weld County, Colorado, clerk and recorder, said. “Her stance on ‘remorse’ is despicable, and she’s doing exactly what we told the governor she was going to do.” Tiffany Lee, the clerk and recorder from La Plata County, told me she and her staff cried with relief when Peters was sentenced. Now she is angry about what she termed Peters’s “sabotage” road show. "I knew for a fact that she would go right back to getting the attention," Lee said.

When I asked Peters what she would say to people who allege that her claims are false, she deflected. “I didn’t create the mistrust,” she wrote in the email. “For years the public got told everything was the most secure ever, and basic questions got treated like a threat. Now a lot of Americans say they don’t trust the process.”

Peters has her own ideas for making elections more secure. “Yelling at citizens won’t fix it. Proof will. Hand-marked paper. Paper poll books. Chain of custody. Counts people can watch, especially in federal races. That’s clearer than black-box machines and electronic poll books,” she wrote. “Making an election observable isn’t an attack on the country. It’s how you earn confidence back.” Election experts mostly dismiss these proposals as impractical, or warn they could produce large-scale errors.

Peters’s podcaster pals, attorneys, and online supporters told me they see her as a symbol of a broader resistance against forces of evil who are attempting to overtake America. “She’s very brave,” Steve Stern, a Republican activist in Broward County, Florida who hosts The Stern American Show on Rumble, told me. (Peters has treated his audience to interviews at least twice since her release.) “She’s trying to do something to help the country.”

Ticktin and another of her attorneys, John Case, told me they have earned no money from representing Peters. “Hopefully someday I’ll get fully compensated,” Case said, laughing. “But it’s doubtful. I’m not doing it for money—I’ll put it that way.” (At one point in his career, he charged $350 an hour.) Ticktin told me the work he’s doing at his own expense to help Peters is bigger than her: It’s about exposing “the biggest crime in the history of the United States—to steal our country.” Peters told me that some of her supporters were misled by fundraising pages that had nothing to do with her. Donations made on her website, she said, help pay for “legitimate costs: legal bills, security when needed,” and travel expenses for her advocacy work.

Her saga damaged some of her relationships with family members, she said. “That still stings,” she wrote. “I’m very grateful for my mom, for the family who stayed, and for the friends and supporters who didn’t throw me away.” She said she is doing ordinary things with family members and catching up on the past two years. When I talked briefly on the phone with her last month, she said she was traveling. “I’ll be in Texas tomorrow; I’ll be in different places the next few days,” she told me, her voice carrying a hint of a southern drawl. She later stressed that she’s traveling for work, not play.

When Peters first hit the election-activist circuit, the movement was dismissed by many elected officials and experts as “fringe.” Six years later, with Trump back in office and election deniers winning races up and down the ballot nationwide, the movement has been mainstreamed within the GOP even as the public’s trust in elections has declined. Their attempts to one day prove that 2020 was stolen may never bear fruit. But activists are already gearing up to uncover the fraud they believe might help Democrats win back Congress in 2026.

entries.title: The Dishonesty of True Crime
entries.summary: The hit Netflix documentary Maternal Instinct tidies a far more complicated story.
entries.content:
The hit Netflix documentary Maternal Instinct tidies a far more complicated story.

On October 9, 2020, Taylor Parker, a 27-year-old mother of two, visited her friend Reagan Simmons-Hancock at her home in northeastern Texas. Simmons-Hancock, who was 35 weeks pregnant with her second child, had something Parker felt she desperately needed: a baby.

What transpired next is the subject of Maternal Instinct, a hit Netflix true-crime documentary directed by Jessica Dimmock and released in June. If you watched the film, you might conclude that you know everything you need to know about Parker and her crimes. But you would be mistaken. What is remarkable—albeit in line with the demands of the true-crime genre—is just how much Maternal Instinct leaves out.

True-crime documentaries are entertainment. They tend to follow a formula with common elements: villains and victims, mystery and suspense, capture and catharsis. These stories typically adopt the tropes of horror films—eerie music, ominous foreshadowing—and offer the prosecution’s version of events, which favor a tidy and dramatic view of a killer’s means and motives. The defense’s job is to poke holes in these assumptions. By omitting vital details from defense teams—in Parker’s case and others—true-crime films portray the grisliest offenses as essentially incomprehensible expressions of wickedness, when the reality is invariably more complicated.

The documentary opens with an acquaintance of Parker’s observing that “there’s evil in our land” and that “evil people do evil things.” This is more of a spiritual explanation than a legal or clinical one. No one can know the fundamental character of another person’s soul, but Maternal Instinct hardly tries to understand Parker’s. Parker is clearly guilty of committing two horrifying murders. Her evident mental illness does, however, challenge the claim that her actions could be explained only by inveterate evil.

As Maternal Instinct recounts, in the months prior to that October morning in Simmons-Hancock’s home, Parker, a divorced mother of two, had staged a fake pregnancy. She had gone to great lengths to convince the people around her—including her fairly new boyfriend—that she was expecting. She’d padded her belly, fabricated medical documents and ultrasounds, and claimed that coronavirus-pandemic restrictions mandated that she see her doctors solo. But unbeknownst to her boyfriend and others, Parker was infertile, having undergone a hysterectomy years earlier.

To keep her lies from being exposed, Parker sought a newborn child to make her own. According to police, she arrived at the house of her very pregnant friend with a scalpel and bludgeoned the 21-year-old Simmons-Hancock with what was likely a hammer, then wrestled her to the floor, sliced her uterus open, and extracted her unborn child. Parker then fled the scene with the infant, leaving Simmons-Hancock to die; the infant died later that day. In 2022, after two years in prison and a weekslong trial, Parker was found guilty of capital murder by a Texas jury and sentenced to death.

Maternal Instinct is meant to paint a portrait of a criminal and her crime, but Parker, who remains on death row, was neither interviewed nor consulted for the documentary—nor were her defense attorneys or their expert witnesses, though Dimmock and her team offered them a chance to comment before releasing the film. Dimmock explained to me that she’d declined to interview Parker out of respect for Simmons-Hancock’s family and friends, and because she doubted that Parker would be truthful or remorseful.

True-crime stories about female killers tend to be especially titillating. Men are about nine times more likely to commit murder than women—who are assumed to be, as the Cornell Law School professor Sandra Babcock put it, “peaceful, nurturing, mothering, caring, obedient.” Murder “seems so out of step with how we view women, how we perceive the stereotypical woman as being,” Babcock, who specializes in gender rights and the death penalty, told me.

Parker’s trial gave rise to a profusion of lurid headlines: “Texas Woman Allegedly Stabbed Mom-to-Be 100 Times, Then Tried to Steal Baby from Womb,” reported People magazine; “Neurologist: Taylor Parker’s Brain Is ‘Broken;’ Defense Rests,” offered the local NBC affiliate KTAL News. Body-cam clips of Parker’s interactions with police spread on YouTube and TikTok. The coverage inspired Maternal Instinct and sets its tone; Dimmock told me that much of her team’s preliminary research into Parker’s case came from the news articles and video clips disseminated online.

Maternal Instinct includes interviews with Parker’s former friends and acquaintances, who describe the broad scope of Parker’s lies over the years, including her many allegedly fictitious ailments and her claims that she was due to receive a multimillion-dollar inheritance from her oil-baron grandparents, who were, in reality, of no particular means. To maintain her deceptions about the pregnancy and other matters, Parker owned multiple cellphones for sending fraudulent messages, fabricated official letters, and used voice-altering software to place anonymous calls.

Randi Chavez, an investigator brought on by Parker’s attorneys, met with Parker for hundreds of hours over the course of a year. Chavez retained experts to assess Parker’s mental and neurological health, and she interviewed people who knew her, including relatives and fellow prisoners. What she discovered was that Parker had displayed symptoms of profound mental illness for many years.

To stipulate that Parker’s mental illness played a significant role in her ghastly crimes is not to suggest that she should have been found either incompetent to stand trial or not guilty by reason of insanity, both of which are exceedingly rare outcomes. Her defense instead presented evidence of her mental illness as a factor that ought to have spared her from the death penalty, but not from punishment altogether. (The American Psychiatric Association, the American Bar Association, and other professional groups have called for a ban on the death penal­ty for those with severe mental illness.) Yet like Parker’s jury, Maternal Instinct does not take Parker to be seriously mentally ill.

At Parker’s trial, the prosecution called upon the forensic psychiatrist Michael Arambula to testify that Parker showed signs of borderline personality disorder, a condition marked by intense mood swings, unstable relationships, impulsivity, fear of abandonment, and feelings of emptiness. But Arambula’s testimony undermined the seriousness of the illness by likening it to intentionally malicious behavior. Borderline personality disorder, he told the jury, is “probably the most manipulative of the personality types.” Parker, he said, had a “pleasant and engaging demeanor atop a core of rage.” He denied that mental illness had contributed to Parker’s murders, insisting to the jury that the uncommon brutality of her crimes did not mean that she was delusional. Members of Simmons-Hancock’s family have likewise adamantly maintained that Parker is “evil” rather than “crazy.”

But Arambula delivered his testimony without ever meeting or interviewing Parker. He drew his conclusions from a review of Parker’s medical records. The defense’s mental-health experts, who’d actually met Parker, came to very different conclusions.

At trial, the defense called a psychiatrist, a neurologist, and a social worker, all of whom confirmed that Parker suffered from a personality disorder that was exacerbated by a personal history of trauma and abuse. They found that Parker’s teenage mother had been negligent, disengaged, and hostile to her daughter before abandoning the family when Parker was a teenager. Her father, meanwhile, had abused methamphetamines, and when Parker was 12, he’d taken her to a house frequented by drug users, where, she said, a man raped her. Maternal Instinct neither reported nor probed those allegations.

After Parker’s conviction, lawyers working on her appeals invited more experts to expand this evidence. Nicole Anders, a clinical psychologist for the defense who met with Parker in January 2025, confirmed that Parker displayed traits associated with borderline personality disorder and argued that this condition—which Anders discussed in the context of Parker’s history of trauma and abuse—significantly altered her ability to reason or function. In a declaration submitted to the court, Anders stated that the trauma and sexual abuse Parker endured as a child had left her hypervigilant, prone to delusion, and desperate for emotional connection. “Although these coping strategies may be maladaptive in the long term,” Anders wrote in her clinical report, “they are rooted in survival instincts. When safe, consistent caregiving is absent or unpredictable early in life, the nervous system adapts to prioritize protection over connection or reason.”

Craig Malkin, a lecturer in psychology at Harvard Medical School, told me that personality disorders form when a patient’s ways of coping with traumatic experiences become deeply ingrained. “We all develop some kind of psychological armor,” Malkin said, which “are just ways of protecting ourselves in vulnerable moments when we’re ashamed, when we fear rejection, when we’re sad and helpless.” For Parker, coping with her mother’s rejection, her father’s destructive irresponsibility, and her own desolate loneliness meant developing delusional fantasies and resorting to extreme people-pleasing behavior. Winning the affection of others sometimes meant lying to them about what she had to offer. Borderline patients, Malkin said, “are people who live on the edge of neurosis and psychosis,” meaning that they alternate between struggling to solve everyday problems and losing touch with reality altogether.

According to experts who spoke with Parker during and after her trial, those delusions centered on her fertility. In 2014, six years before the murders, Parker sought a routine tubal ligation to prevent further pregnancies, but the procedure failed. When a gynecologist confirmed to Parker a year later that she was pregnant, Parker was relieved. She concluded that it was a sign from God that she was meant to have another child. But during a subsequent surgery to remove a cyst on her right ovary, her doctor discovered that the pregnancy was ectopic and developing in her left fallopian tube. While Parker was still under anesthesia, her surgical team procured consent from her then-husband to undertake a total abdominal hysterectomy, removing Parker’s fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and right ovary. Although Maternal Instinct notes that Parker’s hysterectomy left her unable to have children, the film neglects to mention how it happened or how she felt about it.

Parker was shattered when she awoke to find that she could no longer bear children. She confided in friends at the time and later told Diana Barnes, a women’s-mental-health expert brought in by her defense team, that she felt robbed of her identity and purpose in life. She became fixated on pregnancy and childbirth, took a job at a women’s health clinic to be near babies, spent her free time watching mothers and children at parks and stores, and desperately researched surrogacy and uterine transplants, even soliciting her mother for her uterus. As Parker’s obsession progressed, her marriage broke down, and her mental health unraveled. She told others that she had again become pregnant and miscarried, though that was not possible. She told Barnes that when she placed a mock pregnancy belly on her body in 2020, she felt as though it were really her flesh.

Parker was clearly unwell in the months and years leading up to the murders, a fact that Maternal Instinct elides. The documentary suggests that Parker’s crimes were carefully calculated out of selfishness and deceit: A malevolent young woman conspired to entrap her boyfriend with a fake pregnancy and needed a newborn to pull off the plot, so she brutally murdered a friend and stole her baby. But that version of events raises questions that can be answered only by Parker’s mental illness: Why was her desire for love and acceptance so overwhelming that it curdled into criminality? What made the prospect of having a baby with her boyfriend seem worth killing for? Suggesting that Parker’s evil nature alone explains her many schemes and lies is both reductive and unsatisfying.

The film does not explain how someone so adept at weaving elaborate falsehoods might fail to anticipate that staff at the hospital where she arrived with Simmons-Hancock’s baby would also inquire into her own condition. People who had doubted her pregnancy were bound to notice that Simmons-Hancock’s murder and Parker’s “birth” had coincided. But Parker was not thinking clearly, and had not been for some time.

Murder is, after all, not a good idea. Some people commit murder without having thought it through at all, but that sort of crime does not make one eligible for the death penalty. Murders that are eligible for the death penalty involve some degree of premeditation and intent. The presence of planning is usually taken to be proof that a murderer had a sober appreciation for what they meant to do, but it also suggests that something was seriously wrong with their capacity to reason; otherwise, they would have come to the conclusion that, whatever their predicament, murder could only compound it. This does not seem to have occurred to Taylor Parker.

The origins of many murders eligible for the death penalty seem to lie less in deeply rooted inherent wickedness than in particularly compromised minds. Such nuance is usually absent from true-crime yarns, however, because acknowledging mental illness and other impairments complicates simplistic narratives. The genre captivates audiences by dramatizing the worst human behavior, but these stories almost always neglect to illuminate the whole truth, which is stranger and more tragic than what passes for good TV.
